97-004.r: Revolution periods: Jupiter 11.86 years (longest of these); Mars 686.98 days; Earth 365.25 days; Venus 224.70 days.

97-005.r: Jupiter's rings ('Jovian rings') → made of silicates and dust; first found by Voyager 1 in 1979; faint and almost transparent.

97-006.r: Most moons → now Saturn (274); Jupiter, the largest planet, has 97 (as of 27 January 2026) and was the answer when asked.
97-006.c: The book prints (a) Jupiter, correct when the question was set; its own explanation says Saturn now has the most moons, i.e. (c).

98-001.r: Saturn → one revolution around the Sun in about 29.5 years (29.456 years).

98-002.r: Saturn → famous for its rings (seven found; A, B, D, E visible from Earth; looks yellow). Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune also have rings.

98-003.r: Cassini spacecraft → launched October 15, 1997; began revolving around Saturn in June 2004.

98-004.r: Saturn is warmer than Neptune (closer to the Sun). Exception to the distance rule: Venus is hotter than Mercury due to CO2 in its atmosphere.
98-004.h: Planet order: 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles' (Mercury to Neptune).

98-005.r: Titan → largest moon of Saturn (diameter 5,150 km); Rhea is Saturn's second largest (about 1,528 km).

99-001.r: True: Phobos and Deimos are Mars's moons; Neptune has sub-zero methane gas rings. False: hottest planet is Venus, not Mercury; Ganymede (largest moon) is Jupiter's, not Saturn's.

99-002.r: Uranus → 84 years for one revolution around the Sun; a Uranus day is about 17 hours 14 minutes.

99-003.r: Longest year → Pluto (farthest from the Sun among the options): 247.9 Earth years per revolution.

99-004.r: Longest revolution among planets → Neptune (164.9 years). Pluto takes 247.9 years but is not a planet since 2006. Uranus 83.7, Jupiter 11.86 years.
99-004.c: The book prints (d) Pluto, the answer when asked; its own explanation says Pluto lost planet status in 2006, so Neptune (c) is right now.

99-005.r: Neptune → about 165 Earth years per revolution (longest of the planets); eighth and farthest planet; an ice giant with 16 known satellites.

99-006.r: IAU 26th General Assembly (14-25 August 2006) → Pluto removed from the planets and made a dwarf planet.

99-007.r: Smallest planet now → Mercury (4,879 km diameter). Pluto (2376 km) was earlier called the smallest planet.
99-007.c: The book prints (a) Pluto, the old answer; its own explanation says Mercury is now the smallest planet, i.e. (d).

99-008.r: Coldest planet → Neptune (farthest from the Sun); surface about –200 °C; atmosphere of hydrogen, helium and methane.

99-009.r: Pluto's elliptical orbit dips inside Neptune's, so Neptune was farthest 1979–1999, otherwise Pluto. Since Pluto became a dwarf planet (2006), Neptune is the farthest planet.
99-009.c: The book prints (c) 'sometimes Neptune, sometimes Pluto', true when asked; its own explanation says Neptune is now the correct answer.

99-011.r: Pluto (dwarf planet) has five moons, inner to outer: Charon (biggest), Styx, Nix, Kerberos, Hydra.

100-001.r: First manned Moon landing → 20 July 1969, Apollo-11, on the 'Sea of Tranquility'; Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin walked, Michael Collins was the third crew member.

100-002.r: 'Sea of Tranquility' → a dark patch (lunar mare) on the Moon where Apollo-11 landed in 1969; Neil Armstrong stepped out first, then Edwin Aldrin.

100-003.r: Same face of the Moon always faces Earth (A true). But the Moon rotates once in 27 days 7 hours 43 minutes, not 23½ days (R false).
100-003.t: The Moon's rotation and revolution both take 27 days 7 hours 43 minutes; 23½ days is wrong.

100-004.r: Only one Moon face is seen from Earth: its rotation and revolution take the same time (27 days, 7 hrs, 43 minutes). A and R true, R explains A.

100-005.r: Two people on the Moon cannot hear each other → no atmosphere there; sound needs a material medium.

100-006.r: Lunar eclipse → Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon; it happens only on a full moon day.

100-009.r: Extra-bright full moon of 22 December 1999 → Moon at perigee (its closest point to Earth).

100-010.r: Half moon → angle between Sun, Earth and Moon is 90°.

100-011.r: Odd one out → Moon: a natural satellite revolving around Earth; Mars, Mercury and Earth are planets revolving around the Sun.

100-013.r: Planet → Uranus; Satellite → Moon; Comet → Halley (seen 1835, 1910, 1986); Artificial spacecraft → Mariner (Mariner-9 sent to Mars, 30 May 1971).

100-014.r: Blue moon → two full moons in the same month; a full moon comes every 29.5 days, so an extra one builds up about every 2.7154 years.

100-015.r: Object taken from Earth to the Moon → its weight falls to 1/6 (Moon's gravity is 1/6th of Earth's); weight = mass × gravitational acceleration.

100-016.r: Moon–Earth distance → average 384400 km (minimum 363300 km, maximum 405500 km); the nearest option was 364 thousand km.

100-017.r: SELENE ('Kaguya') → Japan's Moon orbiter (14 September 2007), making Japan the first Asian country to put a craft in lunar orbit; it ended at Gill Crater.

101-001.r: Asteroids → small rocky bodies orbiting the Sun between Mars and Jupiter (not Jupiter and Saturn); most are small, some up to 1000 km across.

101-004.r: Asteroids: rocky-metallic, no tail, mostly between Mars and Jupiter. Comets: frozen gases/ice with rock, glowing tail near the Sun, from Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud.
101-004.t: Comets are not found mostly between Venus and Mercury; that statement (2) is false.

102-001.r: Comet's tail points away from the Sun → the Sun's radiation pressure pushes the coma's gas and dust outward.

102-002.r: Hale-Bopp → a long-period comet discovered in 1995 by Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp, named after both.

102-003.r: Comet Shoemaker-Levy-9 → collided with Jupiter during 16-22 July 1994 (found 24 March 1993); first collision of two solar-system bodies seen from Earth.

102-004.r: Meteor ('shooting star') → a small piece of rock from space that glows and burns by air friction on entering Earth's atmosphere; not a star.

103-001.r: Latitude is only North or South of the Equator and ends at the Poles (ninety degrees). So 'forty-five degrees South' is valid; East/West values are longitudes.

103-002.r: Great circle → divides the globe into two halves: the Equator and all meridians (Prime Meridian, any East longitude). No other parallel, e.g. sixty degrees North, is one.

103-003.r: 0° latitude meets 0° longitude (Equator × Prime Meridian) → in the Gulf of Guinea, Atlantic Ocean.

103-005.r: Point near 50°30' N latitude and 5° E longitude → Belgium, so the region is Europe.

103-006.r: Opposite end of the Earth from 30°N, fifty degrees E → 30°S, 130°W (latitude switches N to S; longitude switches E to W).

103-007.r: Northernmost of the four → Rome (highest latitude). North to south: Rome, New York, Beijing, New Delhi.
103-007.t: Don't assume New York lies north of Rome; Rome's latitude is higher.

103-008.r: Longest north-south extent → Chile (continuous mainland) or Russia (if islands are included), so the answer was 'more than one of the above'.

103-009.r: Parallels drawn at 1° interval → 89 in each hemisphere + the Equator = 179.

104-001.r: Cairo, 2 hours ahead of Greenwich → about 30° E longitude (1° = 4 minutes; 120 minutes ÷ 4 = 30°).
104-001.h: Time to longitude: minutes of time ÷ 4 = degrees of longitude.

104-002.r: Noon at eighty-two and a half degrees E (IST meridian) = 6:30 a.m. at 0° (Prime Meridian): the 5 hours 30 minutes gap equals that whole longitude.

104-003.r: 90° difference in longitude → 6 hours time difference (90 × 4 = 360 minutes).

104-004.r: Mid-day at Greenwich and 5 p.m. at a place → 5 hours (300 minutes) ahead, so it lies east: 300 ÷ 4 = seventy-five degrees East.

104-005.r: Prime Meridian (0°, Greenwich; accepted 1884) + the 180° meridian (International Date Line) together form one great circle.

104-006.r: First sunrise of the New Millennium in India → Katchal Island (Andaman and Nicobar), about 1600 km from the mainland and 418 km from Port Blair.

104-007.r: Standard time base → Prime Meridian (0°, Greenwich). It crosses UK, France, Spain, Algeria, Mali, Burkina-Faso, Togo, Ghana; not Niger, Nigeria or Portugal.

104-010.r: GMT time is used in Accra (Ghana), Dublin (Ireland) and Lisbon (Portugal); not in Madrid (Spain).

104-011.r: London, Lisbon and Accra share GMT; Addis Ababa (Ethiopia) is the odd one: its standard time is 3 hours ahead of GMT.

104-012.r: Ahead to behind GMT: Japan +9, Iraq +3, Greece +2, Cuba –5, Costa Rica –6 hours (order 5, 3, 2, 1, 4).

104-013.r: Noon on the IST meridian, 6 a.m. tea elsewhere → 6 hours = 90° west of IST → the place is at 7°30' W.

104-014.r: Telegram sent at noon from Greenwich, 12 minutes in transit, arrives 6 p.m. → 348 minutes of time gap ÷ 4 = 87° E.

104-015.r: International Date Line → runs through the Pacific Ocean, opposite Greenwich; separates two calendar days and bends where land falls in its way.

104-016.r: Date Line lies on the meridian opposite Greenwich → 12 hours (720 minutes) time gap from Greenwich: A and R both true, R explains A.

104-017.r: No 'minimum distance' between two places → along the International Date Line, because it is bent (turned at 8 places, e.g. near Alaska).

104-018.r: Rotation reversed → IST = GMT – 5:30. Noon at the Date Line = midnight GMT, so IST = 6:30 p.m. (18.30 hrs).
104-018.c: The book prints (a) 06.30 hrs, but its own working gives 6:30 pm, which is option (c) 18.30 hrs.

104-019.r: Strait nearest the International Date Line → Bering Strait; Malacca, Florida and Gibraltar straits lie far from it.

104-020.r: Ship crossing the 180 meridian (Aleutians to Dutch Harbour) at 23:30, 1 January 1999 → logs 00:30, 2 January: the Date Line bends around them, so no date change.

104-021.r: Ship sailing west at Earth's rotation speed, 10:00 Monday at 90° W → still 10:00 Monday on reaching the Date Line; 10:00 Tuesday after crossing it.

104-022.r: Anadyr (Siberia) and Nome (Alaska), about 800 km apart across the Date Line → breakfasts fall on different days; Nome is same day or behind, never ahead. Only I correct.

104-023.r: Least-time route for a ship between two places → along the Meridian (book's answer; not sea currents or sea-breeze).

104-024.r: Local time 6:00 AM when GMT is 3:00 AM → 3 hours ahead → 15 × 3 = 45° East.
104-024.h: 1 hour = 15° of longitude; 1° = 4 minutes; east is ahead, west is behind.

104-025.r: Thimphu (Bhutan, 90° E) when Greenwich is 12 noon → 90 × 4 = 360 minutes = 6 hours ahead → 6:00 p.m.

104-026.r: Standard time is man-made (e.g. India uses the 82½° E line), not a natural unit; tropical year, lunar month and day are natural units of time.

104-027.r: More than four time zones (with dependencies) → UK 9, Denmark 6 (with Greenland, Faroe), New Zealand 5, Australia 9; Brazil only four. So four countries.

105-001.r: Equator length → about 40,000 km (40090 km); 78.7% of it passes over water, 21.3% over land.

105-002.r: Equator's 13 countries: Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Gabon, both Congos, Sao Tome, Uganda, Kenya, Somalia, Maldives, Indonesia, Kiribati. Not: Mexico, Venezuela, Brunei, Rwanda, Equatorial Guinea.
105-002.t: Don't be misled by the name: the Equator does not pass through Equatorial Guinea.

105-008.r: Minimum annual range of temperature → at the Equator (Sun's rays almost vertical all year; no winter season).

105-009.r: City nearest the Equator → Singapore (about 1°21' N, only 137 km away); Colombo, Jakarta and Manila lie farther.

105-010.r: Equator, Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn all pass through Africa; South America has only the Equator and Tropic of Capricorn.

105-011.r: Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) → a low-pressure zone at the Equator.

106-001.r: Winter solstice (about 22 December): Sun overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn; noon Sun's altitude at the Tropic of Cancer = 43.0° (the tropics are 47° apart).

106-002.r: Tropic of Cancer does not pass through Iran. It crosses Mexico, Bahamas, Western Sahara, Mauritania, Mali, Algeria, Niger, Libya, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman, India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, China, Taiwan.

107-001.r: Both statements false: day and night come from Earth's rotation; seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis.

107-002.r: Tropic of Capricorn crosses Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina, Chile, Namibia, Botswana, South Africa, Mozambique, Madagascar, Australia (also French Polynesia, Tonga); not Bolivia.

107-004.r: Sun overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn (winter) → North-West India gets colder than the Arabian Sea → high pressure over North-West India.

108-001.r: Equal day and night → equinoxes: 20/21 March and 22/23 September, when the Sun is overhead at the Equator.

108-003.r: Day and night equal (12 hours each) throughout the year → at the Equator.

108-004.r: At the summer solstice (June) the day is still about 12 hours at the Equator; Northern Hemisphere has its longest day, Southern its shortest.

108-005.r: Longest day in the Northern Hemisphere → second half of June (20 or 21 June); in the Southern Hemisphere, second half of December.

108-006.r: Northern Hemisphere: shortest day 21/22 December (winter solstice), longest 20/21 June (summer solstice). Southern Hemisphere: the reverse, longest day 21/22 December.

108-010.r: Smallest noon shadow → 21 June (summer solstice), when the Sun is vertically overhead at the Tropic of Cancer.

108-012.r: 21 June (summer solstice) → the Sun does not set at the Arctic Circle; the Sun is overhead at the Equator only at the equinoxes.

108-013.r: 21 June → over 12 hours of sunlight at the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle (Northern Hemisphere); the Southern Hemisphere has winter with longer nights.

108-014.r: Earth's axis is shifting (I), explained by melting polar ice moving water toward the Equator (III). Solar flares/CMEs (II) are true but affect only the upper atmosphere.

109-001.r: Gas and dust (interstellar dust) hypothesis of Earth's origin → Otto Schmidt. Tidal → James Jeans, Harold Jeffreys. Nova → F. Hoyle, Littleton.

109-002.r: Age of the Earth → found by the uranium dating method.

110-001.r: 'Great Ice Age' → Pleistocene Epoch, from about 2 million to about ten thousand years ago.

110-002.r: Little Ice Age → about 1300 to 1870 A.D. (option 1650–1870 A.D.); Europe and North America had much colder winters than in the 20th century.

110-003.r: Dinosaurs → Jurassic Period (20.8 to 14.4 crore years ago), the 'Age of Dinosaurs'; option: eighteen crore years ago. Remains at Raiyali (Gujarat), Jabalpur (M.P.).

110-004.r: Continents drifted apart → tectonic activities: continents rest on tectonic plates that keep moving.

110-005.r: Gondwana Land (southern part of Pangaea) → South America, Africa, Madagascar, Australia, Antarctica, Arabian Peninsula, Peninsular India; not North America.

110-007.r: Pangaea (Carboniferous, ringed by ocean Panthalassa) split → Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south: South America, Africa, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar, Arabia, Peninsular India).

110-008.r: Cocos Plate → lies between Central America and the Pacific Plate.

110-009.r: Earth's original single landmass → Pangaea, a supercontinent (not Panthalassa, Laurasia or Gondwanaland).

110-010.r: First fossil evidence of life → about 3.5 billion years ago (Archean Eon); no option fits, so the book gives no single answer (*).

110-011.r: Evolution of organisms was influenced by both continental drift and glacial cycles (Savindra Singh, 'Bhautik Bhugol Ka Swarup').

110-012.r: Plate tectonics → crust pieces move slowly, driven by the mantle. Seven major plates: Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Pacific, North American, South American, Antarctic.

110-013.r: Continental drift evidence (all three): matching ancient rocks (about 2,000 million years) of Brazil and West Africa; Ghana gold from Brazil plateau rocks; Gondwana sediments on six southern landmasses.

110-014.r: New crust is added by seafloor spreading; old crust is destroyed by subduction; the two balance, so Earth's size stays the same.

110-015.r: Folding (mountain building) → orogenic force, from interaction of tectonic plates.

110-016.r: Diastrophism → slow or sudden movements of the crust by internal forces (e.g. earthquakes); heterogenic processes do not come under it.
110-016.c: The book gives no single answer (*), though its own explanation names heterogenic processes, option (b), as outside diastrophism.

110-017.r: Dynamic changes on Earth's surface → all six: electromagnetic radiation, geothermal energy, gravitational force, plate movements, rotation and revolution of the Earth.

110-018.r: Chronological order: Sihawal (Lower Palaeolithic) → Patpara (Middle Palaeolithic) → Baghor (Upper Palaeolithic) → Khetaunhi (Neolithic, Microlithic). Code 4, 1, 3, 2.

110-019.r: Order of origin: shelled animals (Cambrian) → first insects → first reptiles → first mammals, i.e. 3 2 1 4 (option c). The book's own order differs.
110-019.c: The standard order is shelled animals → first insects → first reptiles → first mammals, i.e. option (c) 3 2 1 4; the book puts shelled animals too late.

110-020.r: Thar (Rajasthan) desert → Pleistocene and recent deposits; began forming about 70,000 years ago. Pleistocene: 2 million to 10,000 years ago (NCERT).

111-001.r: Igneous rock → cooling and solidification of magma/lava. Extrusive (on the surface, e.g. basalt); intrusive (inside the crust, e.g. granite).

111-002.r: Sedimentary rocks → formed at the surface from weathered older rocks and remains; contain fossils; occur in layers (strata). All four statements true.

111-004.r: Sandstone is layered ('flaky') because it forms underwater (sea or low-lying areas); a sedimentary rock that changes into quartzite.

111-005.r: Chalk → porous and permeable (II true, explains I). Clay → highly porous but least permeable, so 'clay is not at all porous' (III) is false.

111-006.r: Igneous rocks → both crystalline and non-crystalline; made of silicate minerals; no fossils or layers; supply little water.

111-007.r: Granite (igneous, plutonic/intrusive) does not contain fossils; conglomerate, sandstone and shale are sedimentary rocks, which contain fossils.

111-008.r: Metamorphic rocks → formed from either igneous or sedimentary rocks by heat and pressure ('metamorphism' = change of form, Greek).

111-009.r: Granite is igneous, not metamorphic. Metamorphic pairs: granite → gneiss; basalt → schist/amphibolite; shale → slate; limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite.

111-010.r: Odd one out → gneiss (metamorphic, usually from granite); sandstone, limestone and shale are sedimentary.

111-011.r: Rainfall weathers rock: dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid (carbonation, active in limestone) and dissolved oxygen causes oxidation (rust). II and III true, both explain I.

112-001.r: Volcanic products → lava, pyroclastic debris, volcanic bombs, ash and dust, gases (nitrogen and sulphur compounds; a little chlorine, hydrogen, argon). All four listed are.

112-002.r: Basic landform → volcanic cone (lava piled around the vent); residual mountains, monadnocks and erosional waterfalls are products of erosion.

112-003.r: Most abundant volcanic gas → water vapour (H2O); next CO2 and SO2; also H2S, H2, CO, HCl, HF, He.

112-004.r: Highest volcano among the options → Mount Cotopaxi (5911 m); Kilimanjaro 5881 m, Pinatubo 1486 m, Tall 311 m (Philippines).

112-005.r: Most volcanic eruptions → Circum-Pacific belt ('Ring of Fire'): about 75 percent of active volcanoes and most earthquakes.

112-006.r: Molten rock inside the Earth → magma (not lava, basalt or obsidian), so 'None of the above'. Ejected magma = lava; acidic lava is viscous, basic lava fluid.
112-006.t: Magma is inside the Earth; the same material is called lava once it comes out.

112-007.r: Magma solidified deep below the surface → plutonic rocks (slow cooling, large crystals); hypabyssal rocks form at intermediate depth.

112-008.r: No volcanic eruptions in the Baltic Sea (not at a plate edge); volcanoes occur at converging or diverging plate edges.

112-009.r: Mount Etna → active volcano on the east coast of Sicily, Italy (about 3357 m).

112-010.r: Mount Saint Helens → active strato-volcano in Washington, USA (Pacific North West); called the 'Fujiyama of America'.

112-011.r: Mauna Loa ('Long Mountain') → active volcano covering half of Hawaii Island, USA; first well-documented eruption in 1843.
